title: A Ticket Uses a Word You Do Not Know
summary: Practice asking about an unfamiliar term before acting on a ticket.
situation: You are shadowing a mentor and reading a ticket. The ticket mentions a term you do not understand, and you are not sure how it changes the work.
student_prompt: What would you do next before taking action?
safe_actions: Pause and write down the term exactly as it appears.
Check the related training module or glossary if your mentor has asked you to review it.
Ask your mentor what the term means in this local workflow before doing anything with the ticket.
document: The ticket topic or task you were reading.
The unfamiliar term.
The question you need answered before continuing.
ask_mentor_when: The term affects what action should be taken.
You are not sure whether you are allowed to continue.
A user is waiting for an answer you cannot confirm.
avoid: Do not guess what the ticket means.
Do not update, close, or change the ticket until trained and authorized.
Do not tell a user a next step unless a mentor confirms it.
mentor_feedback: A strong answer stops before acting, identifies the confusing term, and asks the mentor for clarification. Learning the language of IT is part of the work.

title: A User Says Their Computer Is Slow
summary: Practice collecting symptoms without jumping to risky fixes.
situation: A user says their computer is running slowly. They are frustrated and want it fixed quickly.
student_prompt: What information would you collect, and when would you ask for help?
safe_actions: Document the symptom in the user's own words.
Ask what the user was trying to do when the slowness happened.
If approved, observe simple facts such as whether the device is powered on, responsive, or showing an error.
document: Device name, asset tag, or location if available.
What the user was doing when the issue appeared.
Any exact error message, timing, or pattern.
What beginner-safe checks were approved and what happened.
ask_mentor_when: The issue may involve user data, accounts, permissions, or software changes.
Approved beginner-safe checks are complete and the issue remains.
The user needs a timeline or answer you cannot confirm.
avoid: Do not delete files to make the computer faster.
Do not reimage the computer as a first step.
Do not change settings or install tools without approval.
mentor_feedback: A strong answer gathers facts, avoids random fixes, and escalates before touching data, accounts, software, or settings.

title: A Printer Is Not Working
summary: Practice safe information gathering for a common support request.
situation: A staff member says the shared printer near their area is not printing.
student_prompt: What can you safely collect or check before asking for the next step?
safe_actions: Ask what the user expected to print and what happened instead.
Record the printer location or visible printer name if available.
If allowed, check simple visible conditions such as power, paper, or an error message on the display.
document: Printer location or visible printer name.
Whether one user or multiple users appear affected, if known.
Any exact error message shown on the printer or user's screen.
What visible checks were approved and what you observed.
ask_mentor_when: The issue may involve print queues, drivers, network settings, or permissions.
The printer shows an unfamiliar error.
The user needs a timeline you cannot confirm.
avoid: Do not change printer drivers, queues, or network settings without approval.
Do not clear or cancel other users' jobs unless trained and authorized.
Do not promise the issue is resolved unless a mentor confirms it.
mentor_feedback: A strong answer records visible facts, avoids system changes, and asks a mentor before touching queues, drivers, permissions, or network settings.

title: You Are Unsure Whether You Can Update a Ticket
summary: Practice preparing a draft note instead of changing official records too early.
situation: You observed a mentor check a monitor issue. You think you know what happened, but you are not sure whether you are allowed to add a note to the ticket.
student_prompt: What would you do with the information you observed?
safe_actions: Prepare a draft note for mentor review.
Include the issue, what was checked, what happened, and what still needs to happen.
Ask your mentor whether the ticket needs an update and who should enter it.
document: The issue or request.
The device or location if appropriate.
The checks you observed or were instructed to perform.
The result and any next step that still needs mentor confirmation.
ask_mentor_when: You have not been trained and authorized to update tickets.
You are unsure whether the issue is resolved.
You do not know what ticket status or wording applies.
avoid: Do not create, edit, close, assign, or update tickets without approval.
Do not write guesses as facts.
Do not mark an issue complete if you are unsure.
mentor_feedback: A strong answer uses a draft note and asks who should update the official system. Drafting is good practice; changing records requires training and approval.

title: A Device Has No Visible Asset Tag
summary: Practice safe equipment identification when tracking information is missing.
situation: You are asked to identify a laptop on the workbench, but you cannot find a visible asset tag.
student_prompt: What should you document, and what should you avoid doing?
safe_actions: Stop and avoid guessing the asset tag.
Record that the asset tag is missing or not visible.
If instructed, collect other visible identifiers such as device location, device name on a label, or serial number.
document: Device type and location.
That no asset tag was visible.
Any other approved visible identifier you were instructed to collect.
Who you asked for the next step.
ask_mentor_when: The asset tag is missing, unreadable, or does not match the task.
Inventory may need to be updated.
You are unsure whether this is the correct device.
avoid: Do not invent or guess an asset tag.
Do not replace or write over an asset tag unless trained and authorized.
Do not move or work on the device if you are unsure it matches the task.
mentor_feedback: A strong answer treats missing asset information as a reason to stop, document, and ask. Accurate identification prevents work on the wrong equipment.

title: You Are Asked to Do Something You Have Not Been Trained On
summary: Practice responding professionally when a task may not be beginner-safe.
situation: Someone asks you to complete a task that sounds important, but you have not been trained on it and do not know whether it is allowed.
student_prompt: What would you say or do next?
safe_actions: Stay professional and explain that you need mentor confirmation before continuing.
Write down what was requested and who requested it if appropriate.
Contact your mentor, IT tech, or supervisor for the next approved step.
document: What task was requested.
What part you are unsure about.
Whether a user is waiting or work is affected.
Who you contacted for approval.
ask_mentor_when: You have not been trained on the task.
The task may involve accounts, permissions, data, imaging, inventory, or official records.
You feel tempted to guess because someone is waiting.
avoid: Do not perform untrained tasks just because they sound simple.
Do not use admin credentials or restricted systems without approval.
Do not promise completion before a mentor confirms the workflow.
mentor_feedback: A strong answer protects the user and the department by asking for approval before acting. Confidence in IT includes knowing when not to proceed alone.
